Guru Har Krishan

Stories of the Sikh Gurus

Guru Har Krishan

The Child Guru

In everyday English — the whole story of the eighth Guru

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story was made to be told. Read slowly, as if you were sitting among family at home — with the hill air of Kiratpur and the lanes of Delhi in the background.

The yellow boxes are the characters speaking in their own words. Change your voice a little when you read them — the little Guru's clear voice, Mata Krishan Kaur's soft one, Ram Rai's heavy one.

(The purple cues) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader, not the listener.

At the end of every part, the green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listener speak. In this story, those questions matter as much as the story.

There are two kinds of things in this book — firm dates and events, recorded in the Sikh records, and stories of the tradition, told in the sangat for centuries. Where a story comes from the tradition, the book says so plainly — 'the tradition tells us'. Where the matter is firm, the book names the date.

This book's main story comes from the Sikh records, the Janamsakhis and the Gurbilas literature, checked against modern scholarship. The full list of sources is at the end of the book.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Guru Har Krishan — the heart of this story. Born in Kiratpur, a Guru at five years old, and gone at seven in Delhi. The eighth Guru of the Sikhs — the Bal Guru, the Child Pir.

Guru Har Rai — the seventh Guru, Har Krishan's father. The Guru of the sangat at Kiratpur.

Mata Krishan Kaur (Sulakhni) — Har Rai's wife, Har Krishan's mother.

Ram Rai — Har Krishan's elder brother. After his father's death he claimed the seat, and he was already favoured at Aurangzeb's court.

Aurangzeb — the Mughal emperor of Delhi. It was he who summoned the Child Guru to Delhi.

Raja Jai Singh — the Raja of Amber, a great noble of Aurangzeb's court. The Child Guru stayed in Delhi at his bungalow — where Gurdwara Bangla Sahib stands today.

Makhan Shah Lubana — the merchant whose test revealed the true Guru at Bakala.

Guru Tegh Bahadur — the son of the sixth Guru, Hargobind, living in the village of Bakala. The ninth Guru after Har Krishan.

Baba Bakala — the village whose name Har Krishan spoke in his last words.

1 · Birth — Kiratpur · · BIRTH — KIRATPUR

In the foothills of the Shivalik hills of Punjab, on the bank of the river Satluj, there was a small town — Kiratpur. The sixth Guru, Hargobind, had founded it, and the seventh Guru, Har Rai, lived there. Cool air came down from the hills, the river water was clear, and the sangat came from far and wide.

There, on 7 July 1656, a son was born to Guru Har Rai and Mata Krishan Kaur. His name was Har Krishan. He was the younger son of the house; there was an elder brother — Ram Rai.

People said the child Har Krishan was not like other children. He was small, but there was a strange peace in his eyes. He did not speak much — but when he spoke, even great men fell silent and listened. In the lanes of Kiratpur he played like any child — but even in play, he was always the first to share.

Mata Krishan Kaur loved her younger son dearly. She said — this child is God's own gift. Guru Har Rai too looked at his younger son and smiled. Little did he know that this small child would one day become the Guru of the whole sangat — and at the age of five.

In those days the life of the sangat at Kiratpur was peaceful. There was kirtan in the morning, the Guru's court by day, and in the evening the sangat sat together and heard the bani. Har Krishan sat beside his father and listened to everything with care — as if he were keeping every word safe inside himself.

At that time the emperor Aurangzeb ruled in Delhi. Har Rai's elder son, Ram Rai, was attached to the Delhi court — and there he had done something that raised questions about his place in the Guru's house. But that story will come later. First, know this — in Kiratpur a small child was growing up, and no one knew how great a burden was going to fall on his shoulders.

The date of birth — two dates

Most sources give Har Krishan's birth as 7 July 1656. Some sources — reckoning by Sawan Vadi 10, Samvat 1713 — give 23 July 1656. This book follows 7 July in the main story, and records the other date here.

His mother's name — two names

Har Krishan's mother is called Mata Krishan Kaur in the sources, and also Mata Sulakhni. Both names are of the same mother — this book uses 'Mata Krishan Kaur' in the main story, and records the other name here.

Pause and think — Har Krishan was a child of five — and one day he had to become the Guru of the whole sangat. Does age alone tell you how wise someone is? Is there a small child around you whose words sound wiser than the grown-ups'?

2 · A Five-Year-Old Guru · · A FIVE-YEAR-OLD GURU

In 1661, Guru Har Rai passed away. Grief fell over Kiratpur. The sangat had only one question — who will be the Guru now?

The elder son, Ram Rai, was there — but he was in Delhi, and his bond with the Guru's house had broken. Har Rai had said plainly in his own lifetime — the seat will go to the younger son, Har Krishan.

And so, in October 1661, a five-year-old child sat on the Guru's seat. The sangat looked at him — a small body, clear eyes, and the Guru's crown upon his head. People said — he is only a child! Can this child be the Guru?

But those who sat in the court saw something else. When the sangat asked a question, the child Guru answered as a great scholar would. When a sorrowful person came, he placed his hand as a Guru of many years would. They say the words of the bani came from his lips as if he had been reading the bani for years.

Once a pandit came — a great scholar, proud of his learning. He said — what can this child know? Debate the scriptures with me. The tradition says Har Krishan explained to him — learning is not what is in books; learning is what softens the heart. The pandit fell silent.

Slowly the sangat came to believe — the Guru's light does not look at age. It is light — and light can burn in any lamp, small or great.

The date of the succession

The date on which Har Krishan became Guru differs between sources — some give 7 October 1661, some 20 October 1661. This book says only 'October 1661' in the main story, and records both dates here.

Ram Rai — why not him?

Ram Rai was the elder brother, but Guru Har Rai had not given him the seat. According to the Sikh tradition, Ram Rai had changed a word of Guru Nanak's bani before the emperor in Delhi to please him — and that is why the Guru's house kept him away from the seat. This is the tradition's telling, and this book tells it as such.

Pause and think — The sangat asked — can a five-year-old child be the Guru? And the Guru's light answered — light does not look at age. In your view, what does it take to be a leader — age, or understanding?

3 · The Child Guru's Court · · THE CHILD GURU'S COURT

After becoming Guru, Har Krishan stayed on at Kiratpur. His court was held — kirtan in the morning, the sangat by day, bani in the evening. People came from far and wide — to see a child on the Guru's seat, and to hear his words.

They say the Child Guru's court was different from the courts of other Gurus. There were no swords here, no horses. Here a child sat, and people sat around him — like a small lamp burning among flowers.

The tradition says that one day a great scholar came — Lal Chand the pandit. He was very proud of his learning. He said — if this child is truly the Guru, let him explain the Gita to me.

Har Krishan smiled and said — explaining the Gita is my servant's work. He called one of his servants — Chhajju, the water-carrier, who did not even know his letters. And the tradition says Chhajju explained the verses of the Gita so well that the pandit's pride crumbled.

The pandit touched Har Krishan's feet and said — I understand now. A Guru is not made by learning — a Guru is made by God's grace.

But the Child Guru's greatest mark was not learning — it was gentleness. Whoever came to him — poor or rich, small or great — he treated them all the same. They say whoever sat beside him found his sorrow grow lighter. That is why the sangat named him the Bal Pir — the Pir of children, and the refuge of the sorrowful.

Guru Gobind Singh later said of him in the Ardas — 'Sri Har Krishan dhiaiyai, jis dithhe sabh dukh jai.' — Remember Har Krishan, at whose sight all sorrows depart. That line is still in every Sikh's Ardas today.

Chhajju and the Gita — the tradition's story

The story of Pandit Lal Chand and of Chhajju the water-carrier explaining the Gita is the tradition of the Janamsakhis and the Gurbilas literature — not a document of history. Its point is that the Guru's light comes not from learning, but from grace.

The line of the Ardas

The line for Har Krishan in the Ardas — 'Sri Har Krishan dhiaiyai, jis dithhe sabh dukh jai' — comes from the Ardas tradition of Guru Gobind Singh, still read in every gurdwara today.

Pause and think — Chhajju did not know his letters — and yet he explained the Gita. Does wisdom come from books, or from the heart? And who is there around you who has not read books, but still speaks words of wisdom?

4 · The Road to Delhi · · THE ROAD TO DELHI

The Child Guru's court was running at Kiratpur — and in Delhi, word reached the ears of the emperor Aurangzeb. Ram Rai, who lived in Delhi, was telling the emperor — the seat is mine; remove the younger brother and make me the Guru.

Aurangzeb decided — summon the Child Guru to Delhi. I shall see for myself whether this five-year-old child is a Guru or not.

The summons reached Kiratpur. The sangat was frightened — calling a child to the emperor's court is no good thing. But Har Krishan said — do not be afraid. A Guru's work is not to fear.

The great noble of the emperor's court, Raja Jai Singh, gave Har Krishan his word — come with me, I shall arrange your stay. And the Child Guru set out for Delhi through Ropar, Banur and Ambala. Wherever he halted on the way, the sangat poured out — people came to see a child Guru.

Reaching Delhi, Har Krishan stayed at Raja Jai Singh's bungalow — the very place where Gurdwara Bangla Sahib stands today. They say Raja Jai Singh's queen wished to test the Child Guru — she hid herself among the servant women, to see whether the child Guru would recognise her or not.

The tradition says Har Krishan walked straight to her and said — Rani Sahiba, why are you hiding here? The queen touched his feet and said — this child is truly the Guru.

But before the meeting with the emperor could take place, something else happened in Delhi — something that changed this story for ever.

Raja Jai Singh and Bangla Sahib

The Child Guru's stay at Raja Jai Singh's bungalow in Delhi is recorded in the Sikh tradition and in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. That very place is Gurdwara Bangla Sahib today, and its sarovar is still sacred to the sangat.

The queen's test — the tradition's story

The story of the queen hiding among the maids and Har Krishan recognising her is the tradition's story — not a document of history. Its point is that the sangat saw in the Child Guru the same light that had been in the earlier Gurus.

Ram Rai and Aurangzeb

Ram Rai's life at Aurangzeb's court and his claim to the seat are recorded in the Sikh tradition. Aurangzeb summoned Har Krishan to Delhi so that he could judge the two brothers' claims — that is the political context, and this book states it plainly.

Pause and think — Ram Rai was the elder brother — and the seat went to the younger. Does being elder by itself give you the right? And when two people claim the same thing, how should the matter be decided — by power, or by truth?

5 · Serving the Sick · · SERVING THE SICK

In 1664 an epidemic had spread through Delhi — smallpox. The lanes were empty, the doors of houses were shut, and people were afraid even to touch their own sick.

And in that same Delhi was the Child Guru — seven years old. And he did what a Guru does — he went to the sick.

The tradition says Har Krishan went from house to house among the sick. He sat beside them, placed his hand on their heads, and gave them water to drink. People said — as soon as the child's hand touched them, the sick felt relief. And those who had run away from their sick out of fear came back when they saw the Child Guru.

Beside Bangla Sahib there was a pond — the sarovar. The tradition says the Child Guru touched the water of that sarovar, and the sangat believes that water carries healing. Even today people carry that sarovar's water home — in memory of that service.

But service has a price — one who goes to the sick may fall sick himself. The Child Guru knew this. Yet he did not stop. The sangat tried to hold him back — Guru Ji, you are small, you will fall ill. Har Krishan said — a Guru's work is service. Running from service is not a Guru's work.

The smallpox epidemic — 1664

In Delhi in 1664 there was an epidemic of smallpox (and, according to some sources, cholera too) — this is recorded in the Sikh records. That Har Krishan served the sick is also recorded.

Service and healing — the tradition's story

The stories of the sick finding relief at the Child Guru's touch, and of healing in the sarovar's water, are the tradition's stories — the sangat's faith, not a document of history. In this book the service is firm, and the healing is told as the tradition's story.

Pause and think — People were running away from their sick — and a seven-year-old child was walking towards them. Does service need courage? And when everyone is afraid, what does one person's stepping forward change?

6 · The Illness · · THE ILLNESS

◆ This part is not for younger listeners

Serving the sick, the Child Guru himself fell ill. He had caught smallpox — the very illness he had gone to save others from.

He was taken to a house near the river Yamuna, so that he could rest. The sangat sat beside him — some reading the bani, some sitting quietly at his side.

The tradition says Har Krishan had a high fever, and sometimes in his delirium he spoke a few words. But when he came to himself, he said only one thing to the sangat — do not be afraid. The Guru's light goes nowhere — it passes from one lamp to another.

The sangat asked — Guru Ji, who will come after you? Har Krishan named no one. He spoke only three words — the words on which the whole story rests.

The illness — the firm fact

That Har Krishan caught smallpox while serving, and fell ill in Delhi, is recorded in the Sikh records. The details of his illness are told in this book in one or two lines, with no account of suffering — which is why this part carries the mark at its top saying it is not for younger listeners.

Pause and think — The Child Guru served others — and fell ill himself. Is that what service means — to help others without thinking of yourself? And is doing that always right?

7 · The Last Words — Baba Bakale · · THE LAST WORDS — BABA BAKALE

On 30 March 1664, in Delhi, the Child Guru Har Krishan left this world. He was only seven years old.

The sangat was weeping. A child Guru had come — and at seven years of age he had gone. People could not understand how it had happened. But before he went, Har Krishan had given the sangat a road to follow.

Before he went, he had said — Baba Bakale.

'Baba Bakale' — it meant that the next Guru would be found in the village of Bakala. But who in Bakala? Har Krishan had named no one — only the village.

The tradition says Har Krishan had said — do not weep when I go. Sing the bani. The Guru's light never dies — it only moves from one place to another.

And so the seven-year-old Child Guru went — but his three words remained. And on those three words rested the sangat's next story.

His age — seven or eight?

Har Krishan's age is given as seven years in some sources and eight years in others. Most sources — including Britannica and SikhNet — give seven years, and the date of death as 30 March 1664. This book follows seven years in the main story, and records the eight-year telling here.

'Baba Bakale' — the tradition's story

Har Krishan's last words, 'Baba Bakale', are the tradition's story, recorded in the Janamsakhis and the Gurbilas literature. The sangat understood these words to mean that the next Guru would be found in the village of Bakala.

Pause and think — Har Krishan named no one — only the name of a village. Is it sometimes right to speak in half-words — so that people must search for the truth themselves? And have you ever solved a riddle whose answer was hidden in a single hint?

8 · The Search at Bakala · · THE SEARCH AT BAKALA

After Har Krishan's passing, the sangat reached the village of Bakala — in Punjab, beside the river Beas. And there they saw a strange sight.

In Bakala, twenty-two men were each calling themselves the Guru. Each one said — I am the true Guru. Each had his own people, his own seat, his own plate. The sangat was bewildered — which of these is the true Guru?

Meanwhile, a man was living quietly in Bakala — Tegh Bahadur. He was the son of the sixth Guru, Hargobind, and Har Krishan's grand-uncle. He said nothing to anyone, sat on no seat — he only read the bani quietly and stayed in meditation.

Then a merchant came — Makhan Shah Lubana. He had been caught in a storm at sea, and he had made a vow — if my ship is saved, I shall give the Guru five hundred gold coins. The ship had been saved. Now he had come to Bakala — to fulfil his vow, and to recognise the true Guru.

The tradition says Makhan Shah went to each claimant in turn and gave each one two gold coins. Each one blessed him and kept the coins — none of them asked what had become of the vow of five hundred.

At last Makhan Shah reached Tegh Bahadur. He offered him two coins too. Tegh Bahadur said — Makhan Shah, you vowed five hundred gold coins — where are the rest?

The ground slipped from beneath Makhan Shah's feet. He ran through the village crying — Guru ladho re! Guru ladho re! — the Guru is found! The Guru is found! And the sangat accepted Tegh Bahadur as the ninth Guru.

But Ram Rai had not given up. He pressed his claim again at Aurangzeb's court — the seat is mine. But the sangat had chosen its Guru — and even the emperor's court could not undo the sangat's decision. Tegh Bahadur became the Guru — and the next story of Sikh history began.

The twenty-two claimants and Makhan Shah — the tradition's story

The story of the twenty-two claimants at Bakala and Makhan Shah Lubana's test is the tradition's story, recorded in the Gurbilas literature and the Janamsakhis. The vow of five hundred coins and the test of two coins come from the tradition, not from a document of history.

Ram Rai's claim — the political context

Ram Rai kept pressing his claim to the seat even after Har Krishan's death, and he had influence at Aurangzeb's court. The sangat accepted Tegh Bahadur as Guru — this is recorded in the Sikh tradition. The tension between the emperor's court and the sangat's decision is stated plainly in this book.

Pause and think — Twenty-two men were shouting that they were the Guru — and the true Guru was the one saying nothing. Is a true leader the one who speaks the most — or the one who speaks the least, but knows the most?

To Think About · · TO THINK ABOUT

Har Krishan's is the shortest story — only seven years of life, only two and a half years on the seat. Yet it tells the greatest thing.

The first thing — the Guru's light does not look at age. A five-year-old child can be a Guru, if God's grace is in him. A leader is made not by age, but by understanding.

The second thing — service itself is the Guru's work. The Child Guru served the sick — and knowing that he himself might fall ill, he did not stop. Service means stepping forward in spite of fear.

The third thing — the true Guru makes no noise. In Bakala twenty-two men were shouting — I am the Guru, I am the Guru. And the true Guru sat in silence. To recognise the truth you need not noise, but a test.

And the last thing — Har Krishan left no bani. There is no composition of his in the Guru Granth Sahib. Yet his name is in every Sikh's Ardas today — 'Sri Har Krishan dhiaiyai, jis dithhe sabh dukh jai.' That means — a story is not made by words alone. A story is made by deeds — and Har Krishan's deed was service.

After Har Krishan came Tegh Bahadur — and his story will come in the next book of this series.

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

The firm dates — the Sikh records

The firm foundation of this book is the dates of the Sikh records — born 7 July 1656, Kiratpur; became Guru in October 1661, at the age of five; died 30 March 1664, Delhi, of smallpox, at the age of seven. These dates are found in sources such as the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism and SikhNet.

The Janamsakhis and the Gurbilas literature

The stories of Har Krishan's life are found in the Janamsakhis and the Gurbilas literature — Chhajju and the Gita, the queen's test, the twenty-two claimants and Makhan Shah's test, and 'Baba Bakale' — all of these are the tradition's stories. In this book each one is named 'the tradition's story' in its own note.

No bani of Har Krishan in the Guru Granth Sahib

Guru Har Krishan left no bani — there is no composition of his in the Guru Granth Sahib. He is the only one of the ten Gurus with no bani in the Granth. That is why no bani of his is quoted in this book — only the line of the Ardas, which comes from the tradition of Guru Gobind Singh.

Modern scholarship

The dates and events in this book were checked against the work of modern scholars — J. S. Grewal, 'The Sikhs of the Punjab'; W. H. McLeod, 'The Sikhs: History, Religion and Society'; Max Arthur Macauliffe, 'The Sikh Religion'; and the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala). Where the scholars and the tradition say different things, both are recorded in this book.

The differences in ages and dates

The sources do not agree on Har Krishan's ages and dates — birth 7 July versus 23 July 1656, the succession 7 October versus 20 October 1661, age seven versus eight years. This book follows one version in the main story, and records every difference in its own note.

One clear thing

In this book Har Krishan is not shown against any faith. He served the sick — without asking whether the sick person was Hindu or Muslim, rich or poor. His message was not to divide, but to join.

The End · · THE END

The story is complete — but the Guru's light is not over yet.

In the next book — Guru Tegh Bahadur, who was found at Bakala, and who gave his head to protect the faith.

Waheguru Ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru Ji ki Fateh.
